name: Amantadine
lead: Amantadine is an oral prescription drug that increases dopamine signalling and blocks NMDA glutamate receptors. It was first approved in the US in 1966 for influenza A and later became a Parkinson's disease medicine [18][1]. In recovery and focus discussions it is known as a dopaminergic drug that has also been used for brain-injury recovery, fatigue and low motivation, which people connect with energy, training drive and presentation.

The US label lists indications for influenza A prophylaxis and treatment and for parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions [19]. Because many circulating influenza strains became resistant, antiviral guidance no longer recommends it for flu, and its main role is neurological [2][3]. Extended-release forms were later approved for levodopa-induced dyskinesia [18].

A multicentre randomised trial of 184 patients with severe traumatic brain injury in a vegetative or minimally conscious state reported faster functional recovery on amantadine than placebo over the treatment period [4]. Registered trials have also tested it for post-COVID fatigue and cognition, cerebral palsy and gait in Parkinson's disease [5][6][7][8].

angle.text: People discuss amantadine as a dopamine-boosting option for fatigue and motivation, which they link to training consistency and appearance. It is a prescription drug used mainly for Parkinson's disease and brain injury.

paras: Against influenza A, amantadine blocks the viral M2 proton channel and so prevents viral uncoating [9][10]. In the nervous system its effects are less fully described and involve enhanced dopamine release, NMDA receptor antagonism and mild anticholinergic action [18].

Approved uses are influenza A and parkinsonism [19]. Reviews cover its place among Parkinson's treatments [11] and among options for dementia with Lewy bodies [12]. Systematic reviews of agitation after traumatic brain injury discuss it among the agents studied [13]. Disorders-of-consciousness guidelines address amantadine after brain injury [14].

Beyond the 2012 brain-injury trial [4], early reports examined amantadine in depression and migraine in 1971 and 1972 [15][16]. Recent trials include extended-release amantadine for OFF-related dystonia [17] and post-COVID fatigue [8][18].

The label lists nausea, dizziness and insomnia as most frequent (5-10%), with hallucinations, confusion, livedo reticularis, orthostatic hypotension and others less often [19]. Deaths have been reported from overdose, particularly with kidney impairment [19]. Animal studies showed embryonic toxicity at high doses [19].

timeline.event: First US approval for influenza A prophylaxis [18].
CDC stops recommending it for influenza due to resistance [18].
NEJM trial in severe traumatic brain injury [4].

card.summary: A prescription dopamine-boosting drug used for Parkinson's and brain-injury recovery and discussed for fatigue and drive.

quick.overview:
Amantadine began as a flu drug in the 1960s and turned out to help Parkinson's symptoms. Today it is mostly a neurological medicine, including for recovery after brain injury.

People interested in energy and motivation talk about it because it raises dopamine activity, which they connect to training drive.
quick.mechanism: It increases dopamine release, blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and has mild anticholinergic action. Against flu it blocks the M2 proton channel.
quick.risks: The label lists nausea, dizziness, insomnia, hallucinations, livedo reticularis and low blood pressure on standing. Overdose deaths are documented, especially with kidney impairment. Prescription-only.
